scope: Long-lever track alignment from the tunnel surfaces, built to extend the modelled corridor beyond the rail anchor span. NOT promoted: it did not clear the forward-prediction bar, so the detector's corridor behaviour is unchanged (no recipe selects it).

module.model: y_s(x) = a_s + b_s x + c x^2, c shared across surfaces, (a_s,b_s) free per surface
module.why: The lining is an extrusion of one profile along the alignment, so every longitudinal surface carries the same curvature with its own offset. Offsets are never combined (that is what wrecked per-bin medians); curvature is pooled, which is what buys precision.
module.rails_role: included as one more surface with weight 4, anchoring offset and heading near field

measured_estimator.fits_available: 5 of 11 sampled frames on roundT_doubleT (else 'only 1 usable traces': chaining breaks)
measured_estimator.status: precision is sufficient; availability is not

forward_prediction_abs_error_m.method: Predict the centre-line ahead from a source frame, express that world point in the axes of a later frame that has driven over the same ground, compare with the rails it measures there.

conclusion: The binding limit beyond ~100 m is the model class, not the estimate: a single local quadratic fitted to any evidence is 20-38 m off at 200-250 m in these recordings, while its own statistical error would allow 0.5 m. The alignment's curvature changes along the stretch (randomT junctions, transitions), so a per-frame smooth continuation cannot carry 300 m - and no amount of extra surface evidence changes that.
next_architectures: Incremental alignment tracker: carry position/heading/curvature as state across scans, predict, correct against the measured rails near field and the surfaces at range, and publish the corridor from the filtered state. This can follow changing curvature, which a per-frame fit cannot; it needs the same forward-prediction test as its acceptance bar.

Far-field decision without a corridor: test track-bed and rail continuity (a foreign object interrupts the bed/rail line, and the bed returns to 200+ m). Catches objects on the track without absolute alignment, but not objects sitting inside the envelope beside it.
not_claimed: No corridor widening, no threshold change, no recipe selects the estimator.
The 200-250 m rows rest on one sample each; they bound the model, they do not calibrate it.
Surface availability (5/11 frames) would have to be fixed before any promotion.
No estimator in this module is used by the detector; the spline was measured unfit and left unselected.

single_quadratic_shared_curvature.signature: fits well, wrong function class beyond ~100 m

penalized_spline_shared_function.why_tried: a single quadratic cannot follow an alignment whose curvature changes; a spline with a second-difference penalty can, in principle, and its posterior covariance gives the horizon
penalized_spline_shared_function.verdict: Unfit even with maximum flexibility, so the failure is not the alignment model but the trace extraction below it: per-bin Cartesian clustering follows the nearest cluster, so a 'surface' hops between wall, cable tray, floor junction and far bore as the bin slides, and no shared function can absorb that. Residuals of metres are the symptom.

diagnosis.representation: The scan is a 2D angular grid. Clustering points in Cartesian space and chaining them longitudinally is the wrong primitive for a tunnel filled with attachments.
diagnosis.correct_primitive: Range image: per azimuth column the elevation profile is a cross-section. Tunnel alignment and convergence are extracted by matching/tracking consecutive cross-section profiles (correlation of profiles, not points), which is robust to attachments because an attachment perturbs a few profile samples, not the profile's centre.
design: form the range image from the scan's ring/azimuth structure
per column, extract the cross-section profile and its centre by correlation with the neighbouring columns
track centres along the tunnel into an alignment state (position, heading, curvature), filtered across scans
project the corridor from that state and set the horizon from its covariance
acceptance: the same forward-prediction test, <=0.5 m at 100 m and <=1 m at 200-300 m

rail_head_returns_per_20m_bin.frame: roundT_doubleT frame 0, band = head height +/-0.12 m above the local bed, |y - centre| < 1.0 m

observability_limits.conclusion: The track itself - rails and bed - becomes unobservable beyond roughly 50-90 m in these recordings, because the rings that would sample a gauge-wide strip at that range are one or two. No alignment estimator can measure the track there; it can only infer it from the tunnel.

circle_fit_axis.why: a circle through two walls, a flat floor and an arched ceiling sits about a metre off the track centre, and that bias changes where the section changes; calibrating it on the rails over 0-40 m leaves 1.3 m of drift by 60-100 m

tunnel_as_proxy.conclusion: The tunnel substitutes for the track at no better than about 1.3 m, which is 85% of the 1.535 m corridor half-width, and it degrades with range: at 150-250 m every model tried is 5-41 m off.

verdict.goal_as_stated: A clearance-certified gaбарит at 100-300 m on curves is not achievable on these recordings. The binding constraint is physical observability, not the estimator: the track is not measured beyond ~50-90 m, and the tunnel's centre is biased against the track by ~1 m with a drifting bias.
what_is_deliverable: Short-range clearance (within the validated horizon, ~65 m) with the curvature continuation already shipped.

Far-field presence and range: an object at 150-250 m that stands into the beam fan is measured directly in range and lateral offset in the sensor frame; what cannot be certified there is its relation to the track centre. Reporting presence/range with the clearance relation flagged unknown is honest and is what the organizers score (distance and presence), while never claiming a clear route from unmodelled coverage.
what_would_be_needed_for_certified_300_m: More returns at range (a sensor with denser beams or a longer baseline), or
an external alignment source (survey, previous passes, GNSS/IMU-fused map) - i.e. a track database rather than a per-scan estimate, or
a vehicle model that bounds where the vehicle may be within the observed tunnel envelope, converting the unmeasured track into a bounded swept-volume claim instead of a centre-line claim.

uncertainty_calibration.method: tunnel_guard.uncertainty_probe: claimed sigma_path vs measured centre error, label-free pair test
uncertainty_calibration.finding: The fit-covariance sigma propagated by _continuation is over-confident by 1.6x at 50-60 m and 4-8x at 80-150 m, because model error (the quadratic not holding as the alignment changes) dominates statistical error. The existing heuristic term 0.06+0.008r+0.0003r^2 tracks the measured error within 0.46-1.34x over 10-110 m of extrapolation, so it is the better-calibrated model and is what both backends already use.

horizon_policy.binding_knob: path_max_uncertainty_m = 0.4 (not path_max_extrapolation_m; raising that gate 25 -> 45 changed nothing)

effect_roundT_doubleT.note: two frames become certified obstacles in a band where the centre is uncertain by ~1.0 m (65% of the half-width)

alternative_measured.decision: rejected: it manufactures certified claims where the alignment is least certain, for no measured gain

vertical_alignment.bed_anchors_per_frame: 13-18, extending to 65-105 m (the floor is wide, so it is sampled far beyond the rails' 40 m)
vertical_alignment.verdict: Inside its own 15 m gate (ground_max_extrapolation_m) the linear bed extrapolation errs by <=0.02 m, so the corridor's vertical placement is sound: heights are referenced to a surface measured to 65-105 m. The binding unknown at range is lateral, not vertical.
vertical_alignment.scoring_implication: Range is measured directly and height above the running surface is known to ~100 m, so far-field presence and height are usable; only the lateral track relation is unmodelled beyond the 74 m horizon.

far_field_reporting.definition: the path uncertainty the classifier itself used at that object's distance, so the stated uncertainty and the decision are consistent by construction: sqrt(base^2 + extension^2) with base = 0.06 + 0.008r + 0.0003r^2 (calibrated 0.46-1.34 against measured error over 10-110 m of extrapolation) inside the modelled horizon, and null beyond it
far_field_reporting.why_null: beyond the horizon the corridor is not used for any decision, and reporting a finite number there would imply knowledge that does not exist; null states 'lateral track relation unknown'
far_field_reporting.earlier_version_rejected: a 4.1e-4 * d^2 model was first used and rejected: it understates uncertainty at short extrapolation (0.04 m where the measurement said 0.19 m)
far_field_reporting.not_claimed: reporting only: no decision, threshold or status changed, verified on 200 frames

forward_prediction_powered.recording: roundT_doubleT, 24 source frames (every 10th), poses from build/perf-cpp-opt-20260917
conclusions: the shipped curvature continuation is 2.4x / 3.4x / 5.2x / 2.9x better than the old straight continuation at 40 / 50 / 60 / 100 m
the bore axis is worse than the shipped model at every range measured (1.9-8.3 m) - confirmed dead at sample size, not just anecdotally

the surface long-lever model wins at 100 m (0.523 m) but is worse than the shipped model by 120 m (6.299 vs 3.502) and stays worse: its advantage does not persist, so it was measured and declined rather than wired in (a new per-frame surface extraction plus a C++ kernel path for at most ~15 m of horizon)
beyond 100 m every model is >= 3.5 m off, i.e. >= 2.3x the 1.535 m corridor half-width; at 180 m the best is 9.886 m (6.4x)
caveats: single recording for the far rows; the fine ordering at 40-60 m has n = 13-20 and is not separable between the shipped and surface models there

temporal_history_estimate.hypothesis: the alignment is smooth along arc length and the train accumulates rail measurements over its whole driven stretch (250 m here), so curvature change along the route - invisible to a single 40 m scan - might be recoverable from history and extrapolated forward
temporal_history_estimate.method: tunnel_guard.history_probe: rail centre-line samples from frames up to the current one, transformed into the current sensor frame through the recorded poses, fitted with a cubic and evaluated at the look-ahead; strictly causal, validated against later frames' rails
temporal_history_estimate.conclusion: Worse than the shipped single-scan model at every range and every history length. These routes are sequences of independent curves, straights and junctions (roundT/squareT/pressureGate), so the alignment already driven does not determine the alignment ahead - the same reason a single-scan quadratic fails, only stronger because more history means more irrelevant geometry.

information_limit.statement: On this sensor and these routes the future lateral alignment is an *information* limit, not an estimation limit: the only signal that reaches 200 m is the tunnel lining, which is biased against the track centre by ~1 m with drifts; the track's own signature dies at 40-90 m; and the alignment's future curvature is not a function of anything measured (independent curves and junctions). No estimator can extract information the sensor never captured.
strategies_tested_and_rejected: per-scan quadratic from the anchor window (shipped: best, but a 40 m lever)
shared-curvature quadratic over surface traces plus rails (wins at 100 m, worse by 120 m)
penalized spline with per-surface offsets (cannot fit the traces: 1.7-4.5 m residual with no penalty)
robust circle fits to perpendicular slabs / calibrated bore axis (1.9-8.3 m at every range)
uncertainty propagation from the fit covariance (over-confident 1.6-8x; honest bound exceeds the tunnel width)
cumulative temporal rail history (worse at every range; past alignment does not determine future alignment)
